questions.q: What are the four real components a useful postmortem must include?
options: A factual timeline, the actual root cause, how it was resolved, and concrete prevention follow-up
A status update saying the issue is fixed, with no further detail
A list of every user who reported the incident
An apology and a promise it won't happen again
questions.explain: Skipping any one of the four leaves the document unable to actually explain or prevent a recurrence.

questions.q: Why is "response times tripled for 45 minutes" a symptom rather than a root cause?
options: It restates what was observed without explaining the actual mechanism that caused it, such as a specific unoptimized query consuming semaphores
It is actually a complete and sufficient root cause on its own
Symptoms and root causes are interchangeable terms with no real difference
Only error messages can ever qualify as root causes
questions.explain: A postmortem that stops at the symptom hasn't explained anything new — the root cause names the actual chain of cause and effect.

questions.q: Why does "we'll be more careful with deployments going forward" fail as a prevention action?
options: It names no specific change, owner, or deadline, so it commits nobody to anything and changes nothing about the process
It is actually the strongest possible prevention action a postmortem can include
Prevention actions are never necessary once an incident is resolved
ServiceNow Support requires that exact phrase in every postmortem
questions.explain: A concrete prevention action names a specific change, a specific owner, and a specific deadline — vague intentions change nothing.

questions.q: What does a blameless postmortem focus on, per this lesson?
options: What in the process or system allowed the incident to happen, rather than which individual was at the keyboard
Identifying exactly which person should be disciplined
Avoiding any factual timeline so no one feels targeted
Keeping the root cause vague to protect the team
questions.explain: Asking what gap in review or testing let a problem through has an answer that actually prevents recurrence; naming an individual does not.

questions.q: Why does blaming an individual in a postmortem actually make future incidents worse, per this lesson?
options: People stop volunteering details and describe incidents vaguely, which slows down the investigation a postmortem depends on
It has no real effect on how people report future incidents
It guarantees the same individual will never make another mistake
It is required by ServiceNow's platform architecture
questions.explain: Expecting blame makes people withhold the honest detail postmortems need, which is why the blameless principle is a practical requirement, not just courtesy.
